title: Forest or tundra? How different vegetation reconstructions of Last Glacial landscapes in Europe may shape our perception of early human dispersal processes
abstract: ABSTRACT Regional variability and long‐term changes of past ecosystems likely had a strong impact on hunter–gatherer population dynamics, including the expansion of anatomically modern humans and the disappearance of Neanderthals. However, our understanding of these ecosystems remains limited, even when looking at large‐scale patterns, such as the extent and distribution of forested areas. Vegetation reconstructions are key to better understanding ecological preferences and their influence on the spatial distribution and dispersals of early humans. Here, we compare four different vegetation reconstruction techniques, two based on pollen data and two vegetation models, between 70 and 20 thousand years before present in Europe. Absolute values in forest cover can differ by up to 40% between reconstruction techniques, highlighting that the choice of method can make the difference between a boreal forest and a tundra. Besides method‐specific and statistical uncertainties, the reason for such a substantial offset lies in the loose definition of forest cover metrics, rendering a direct comparison between methods impossible. At the same time, we show that all reconstruction techniques accurately reconstruct ecosystem dynamics over time on continental to regional scales. We therefore highly recommend that researchers use relative forest cover measures as the more robust method to estimate past landscapes.

title: Sensitivity of the IceCube atmospheric muon rate to decadal trends in the effective atmospheric temperature
abstract: arXiv:2611.00918v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Decadal changes in the Antarctic stratosphere, generally associated with ozone recovery and shifts in polar circulation, are of broad geophysical interest. However, independent long-term measurements of the atmosphere above the Antarctic interior are scarce. We assess whether the atmospheric muon rate recorded by IceCube could constrain decadal changes in the effective atmospheric temperature, $T_\mathrm{eff}$, a weighted average of temperature through the atmosphere that is most sensitive to the stratosphere. Using public atmospheric reanalysis data and records of cosmic-ray, solar, and geomagnetic variability, we reproduce the measured seasonal response of the IceCube muon rate. We then test whether the same response applies to long-term temperature changes with a different vertical temperature profile. The limiting requirement is detector stability rather than counting statistics: an unmodeled muon rate drift of $1\%\,\mathrm{decade^{-1}}$ would mimic a temperature trend of $2.8\,\mathrm{K\,decade^{-1}}$. The long-term rate must therefore be stable to approximately $0.3\%\,\mathrm{decade^{-1}}$. Within this budget, snow accumulation contributions can be constrained. For a 14-year record, atmospheric variability gives a one-sided 95% CL statistical sensitivity of $1.6\,\mathrm{K\,decade^{-1}}$. Given this sensitivity, the $\sim0.9,\mathrm{K,decade^{-1}}$ cooling indicated by the 2011-2025 atmospheric records would be constrained at the 95% confidence level after approximately 22 years of measurement.

title: Temporal variability of mineral dust composition on an alpine snowpack in the Tateyama Mountains, Japan
abstract: Mineral dust is one of the major light-absorbing impurities in snow and ice, and affects snowpack and glacier melting. However, the origin and composition of mineral dust deposited on snow surfaces, and how these vary over time and space, remain poorly understood. This study examined the temporal and spatial variability in the composition of mineral dust in an alpine snowpack in the Tateyama Mountains, Japan and evaluated the relative contributions of long-range-transported and locally derived dust to dust deposition on the snow surface. Surface snow samples collected from April to July were analyzed using microscopy, SEM–EDS, and X-ray diffraction (XRD). The results showed a clear temporal transition in the mineral assemblages. The April samples were dominated by quartz and feldspar, consistent with long-range-transported Asian dust. Conversely, samples from May to July showed increasing abundances of chlorite, biotite, and amphibole, indicating a growing contribution of locally derived dust during the melt season. Coarse, feldspar-rich dust was frequently observed near diorite outcrops. These results indicate that Asian dust dominated in spring, whereas locally derived dust increasingly contributed to the mineral composition of surface snow during the melt season. This suggests that local geology plays an important role in controlling snowpack impurity composition, with potential implications for snow-surface radiative properties.

title: Reconstructing Boundary Layer Wind Profiles with Machine Learning: A Comparative Study on IGRA Radiosonde Data
abstract: arXiv:2611.13359v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Wind profiles in the atmospheric boundary layer (ABL) drive short-range forecasting and wind-energy siting, yet sparse radiosonde coverage forces practitioners to interpolate them from a handful of physical predictors. We benchmark modern tabular learners against analytical parameterizations on 158,097 IGRA soundings. CatBoost, TabM, and FT-Transformer reduce RMSE to 1.3-1.6 m/s, against approximately 3 m/s for power-law and Monin-Obukhov fits; once the predictor set is fixed the three architectures differ by less than 0.05 m/s, so accuracy is driven by predictors rather than architecture. A cohort analysis of within-bin profile dispersion places an empirical floor of approximately 1.77 m/s on any point-wise predictor that uses standard radiosonde features, consistent with prior eddy-viscosity inversions. A one-dimensional Fourier Neural Operator applied as a post-hoc corrector to frozen tabular predictions reduces near-surface RMSE on U.S. stations from 1.5 to 1.2 m/s, while leaving upper-layer error unchanged. Further gains should come from new predictors rather than larger models.

abstract: Offshore the Horn of Africa, volcanic ash layers preserved in deep-sea sediments have played a crucial role in establishing and refining chronologies for paleontological sites in the East African Rift System (EARS). However, no such layers younger than 750 ka have been identified, despite evidence for major eruptions during this interval. Here, we investigate the 166-150 ka interval in marine sediment core MD96-2073, retrieved near Socotra Island. We constructed an age-depth model based on δ 18 O tie-points and 14 C dates, using Bayesian statistics (BACON software). This core spans at least 250 kyr, with a mean chronological uncertainty of ± 3.5 ka (95% confidence interval). Although no visible tephra layers were identified, glass-shard counting revealed a distinct cryptotephra horizon dated to 154.6 ka (13 ka as whole 95% confidence interval). Major and trace element analyses of glass shards allow correlation of this cryptotephra with the Konso Silver Tuff, which is considered to derive from the Shala volcano, making it the youngest EARS-derived tephra currently correlated with marine deposits. This cryptotephra represents a widespread tephrostratigraphic marker and provides a new chronological anchor for sediments of comparable age, including lacustrine, paleontological, and archaeological records.

title: Evaluating the Behavior of 230 Th and 3 He Constant‐Flux Proxies Across a Carbonate Preservation Gradient in the Cocos Ridge
abstract: Abstract We present a comparison of extraterrestrial 3 He ( 3 He ET ) and excess 230 Th ( 230 Th xs ) as constant flux proxies across a depth transect on the Cocos Ridge, evaluating their behavior as a function of carbonate dissolution and lateral sediment redistribution. Overall, 60% of paired 3 He ET ‐ and 230 Th xs ‐derived mass accumulation rate (MAR) estimates overlap within 1σ uncertainty, indicating broad agreement between the two systems. However, statistically significant discordances between He‐ and Th‐derived MARs occur in three of four cores, with He‐derived MARs exceeding Th‐derived MARs at the ridge crest (positive ΔMAR values) and falling below Th‐derived MARs at flank sites (negative ΔMAR). The discordance at the ridge crest is consistent with sediment winnowing and preferential removal of 3 He‐bearing particles, whereas the smaller discordances in flank cores are best explained by a complementary focusing signal, likely reflecting redistribution of material removed from the ridge top. Evaluation of the negative ΔMAR offsets demonstrates that 230 Th xs is effectively retained during carbonate dissolution, as ΔMAR responses remain small despite strong CaCO 3 preservation gradients, and theoretical constraints indicate negligible thorium mobility. When applied jointly, the two proxies provide complementary constraints on MARs that would remain unresolved using a single proxy. However, their interpretation remains site‐dependent, requiring careful consideration of sediment composition, transport regime, and analytical limitations. Because sedimentary burial fluxes are calculated from component concentrations and MAR, these proxy‐dependent differences directly affect estimates of carbonate and other elemental burial fluxes, with implications for reconstructing both past and modern marine biogeochemical cycles.

title: Early winter underestimated Indian Ocean teleconnections to the Northern extra-tropics in seasonal forecast models
abstract: Abstract There has been increased attention to the Indian Ocean as a source of predictability for the early winter climate over the North Atlantic European (NAE) region in the form of a North Atlantic Oscillation (NAO)-like pattern. Particularly, the October Indian Ocean Dipole (IOD) triggers a delayed precipitation response over the Indian Ocean in early winter, which mediates the Rossby wave that propagates to the NAE sector. Seasonal forecast models have been found to be severely underestimating this teleconnection, and finding the underlying causes is crucial to the improvement of the models’ performance. We demonstrate that models lack an adequate December Indian Ocean convective response, both in terms of magnitude and spatial pattern. This misrepresentation of the heating influences the generation of Rossby Wave Source (RWS) along the subtropical jet. Employing a dry linear baroclinic model, we also find that the December upper-tropospheric mean state does not support accurate downstream wave propagation in the forecast models. Particularly, a combination of a stronger subtropical jet and erroneous polar waveguide zonally traps the wave train in the models. Furthermore, our linear model simulations also suggest that this inaccurate downstream wave propagation potentially affects the strengthening of the wave over the North Pacific.

title: Extremes, Teleconnections, and Trends in Growing Season Precipitation over the Corn Belt, 1182–2023 CE
abstract: Abstract Tree-ring chronologies were used to reconstruct growing-season precipitation for the North American Corn Belt from 1182–2023 CE. The reconstruction explains close to 60% of the variance in instrumental May–July precipitation totals (1901–2014) and reproduces the teleconnections with circulation and surface climate variables detected in the instrumental precipitation data, substantiating the skill of the reconstruction and indicating episodic co-occurrence of drought between major crop production regions of the central United States and Eurasia. The episode with five consecutive years of deficit May through July precipitation totals in the Corn Belt from 1930–1934 during the Dust Bowl drought was exceeded by several uninterrupted droughts reconstructed during the pre-instrumental period. The early 17 th century drought (1627–1639) was the most severe, sustained, and unbroken drought in the reconstruction for at least 600-years and has no analog in the modern instrumental observations. This drought coincided with decadal dryness in China and eastern Europe and provides a paleoclimatic example of simultaneous megadrought in major breadbasket regions of Eurasia and North America. The decade of wetness during the early 21 st century in the instrumental observations appears to have been unmatched for 700-years and may have been enhanced by increased humidity and radiation changes associated with the dramatic intensification of agriculture in the Corn Belt.

abstract: We developed a new global ocean model to understand how mercury moves and changes in seawater. The model closely matches observed mercury patterns, providing confidence in its results. It will serve as the ocean part of a fully coupled Earth system mercury model (CESM2-Hg) with air, land, and river processes, improving predictions of future mercury pollution and guiding strategies to protect marine life and human health.

title: Estimating ensemble-mean anomaly correlations and the ratio of predictable components using an unbiased estimate of the predictable signal variance
abstract: arXiv:2611.07878v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The correlation ($r$) between ensemble mean forecasts and observations is a frequently-used metric of forecast quality in the weather and climate prediction communities. However, uncorrected estimates of $r$ are biased towards zero at finite ensemble size due to the influence of unpredictable noise that contaminates the sample ensemble mean. This note summarises established ensemble-size adjustment methods and characterises the behaviour of $r_{\infty}$, a correlation estimator that is constructed from an unbiased and ensemble-size-independent estimate of the signal variance. The only requirement is that forecast members are exchangeable with one another such that they can be interpreted as independent draws from a case-specific predictive distribution. The estimator $r_{\infty}$ does not require forecasts and observations to be statistically exchangeable, only that the unpredictable component of each member is uncorrelated with the observed truth, and thus works for both reliable and unreliable forecasts. In some situations, $r_{\infty}$ may be undefined (i.e. the estimated signal variance is negative) or fall outside the admissible range $-1 \leq r_{\infty} \leq 1$ when the predictable signal is small relative to the sampling uncertainty. These inadmissible values can be interpreted as evidence that the true predictable signal cannot be resolved with the available ensemble size and number of cases. The same unbiased signal variance can also be used to estimate the correlation between the predictable signal and individual members to yield an ensemble-size-invariant estimator of the ratio of predictable components (RPC). In contrast, variance-based RPC estimates, including forms that correct only the model predictable component, are biased low by a factor that depends only on the ensemble size and model signal-to-noise ratio.

title: A Land-Sea Contrast Pattern in Surface Temperature and Atmospheric Circulation Trends in Recent Decades
abstract: arXiv:2606.19581v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We argue land-sea contrast is an important driver of spatial patterns of observed surface temperature and atmospheric circulation trends, including the negative Inter-Decadal Pacific Oscillation (IPO)-like tendency across the Pacific basin. Observed and modeled trends display an overall decline in sea level pressure over the faster-warming land, with a spatial pattern that resembles the seasonal cycle and modeled response to land heating. Coupled historical forcing climate model simulations underestimate the land-sea warming ratio. It is only in the early response of abrupt CO2 quadrupling climate model simulations that climate models are able to recreate the observed land-sea warming ratio, in which case a negative IPO-like sea level pressure trend and surface warming pattern over the Pacific comparable to observed trends are seen. We propose that some discrepancies between observed trends and those predicted by climate models are explained by the underestimation of the land-sea warming ratio by climate models.

title: Unreported mass movement cascades and future Glacial Lake Outburst Flood (GLOF) hazard in Jammu and Kashmir, Western Himalaya
journal: Natural hazards and earth system sciences
abstract: Abstract. The Warwan sub-basin in Jammu and Kashmir is a remote glaciated region containing several glacial lakes and has recently experienced population growth and infrastructure development. Due to inaccessibility and geomorphic masking, multiple mass movement events including avalanches and Glacial Lake Outburst Floods (GLOFs) have remained largely unreported. This study analyzes three major avalanche events from the past two decades. The September 2005 and September 2020 avalanches originated from glaciers GL-B and GL-A within the same glacier complex, while the March 2020 rock–ice avalanche initiated from the headwall of glacier GL-F in an adjacent valley and terminated before reaching its ablation zone. Runout mapping shows that the September 2020 avalanche descended from the headwall of GL-A and impacted its proglacial lake, triggering a GLOF. In contrast, the September 2005 event terminated before reaching the glacial lake that began forming in 1999 at the terminus of GL-B. Geomorphic analysis indicates persistent sediment influx from meltwater streams of GL-D and GL-E into the lake associated with GL-A, progressively infilling the basin. Continued glacier retreat caused meltwater to accumulate behind the sediment infill, dividing the basin into two disconnected lakes. Impact from the September 2020 avalanche led to complete drainage of stored water and sediment, generating a downstream debris flow. Pre- and post-GLOF imagery reveals breaching and widening of the outflow channel and deposition of a debris fan downstream. The repeated history of mass movements and continued growth of glacial lakes raise serious hazard concerns in the Warwan sub-basin. GLOF modeling identifies Lake-B as potentially hazardous lake at the present condition posing significant downstream risk. Settlements such as Youdu and Qaderna, along with bridges, roads, and residential structures, lie within potential GLOF inundation zones. High sediment availability from past mobilization and deposition along the valley increases the potential of debris flow cascades, posing elevated risks to downstream infrastructure and hydropower, underscoring the need for preparedness and mitigation planning. GLOF modeling suggest that early warning system closer to the source will be able to provide a good lead time in case of potential GLOFs in the valley.

title: Glaciotectonic Spectrum
journal: Transactions of the Kansas Academy of Science
abstract: Glaciotectonic landforms include a spectrum of hill-hole pairs, composite ridges, push moraines, cupola hills, and drumlins with deformed internal structures. Their regional distribution as well as buried glaciotectonic features are reviewed with an emphasis on Scandinavia, adjacent Russia, and Baltic nations. LiDAR and ground investigations were the keys for recognizing murtoos as a new category of distinct glaciotectonic landforms, which are particularly well documented in Finland and Sweden. Three main zones of glacial landscapes are recognized for ice-sheet glaciation - outer, intermediate, and inner, as well as a transitional boundary between the outer and intermediate zones. Glaciotectonic phenomena are numerous and widespread in all of these zones wherever the substratum consists of sedimentary bedrock or unconsolidated sediments.

title: A surge-detachment sequence at Dehdal Glacier in the Pamir Mountains, revealed by daily PlanetScope imagery
abstract: This study investigates a rapidly surging glacier in the Pamir Mountains using daily satellite imagery and unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) data. It reveals that a surge-detachment sequence can rapidly displace ice downstream and transform valley morphology. The findings show that even small glaciers can produce large, rapid environmental impacts and highlight the need for detailed observations to understand glacier instability and improve hazard assessment in a warming climate.

title: Improved rainfall forecasts in daily use over East Africa
abstract: arXiv:2512.24525v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Ensemble forecasting has proven to be a vital tool for predicting extreme, life-threatening or only partially predictable weather events. As well as providing probabilistic products, individual ensemble members provide context and realisations of possible extreme weather. However, many National Meteorological Services in East Africa lack the computing resources required to run their local area models in ensemble mode over the full period of the two-week medium range. In this paper we test the performance of a short and medium-range forecast system recently put into daily use, comprising the global ECMWF ensemble forecast, post-processed using cGAN, a neural network model. We find that cGAN achieves probabilistic forecast skill comparable to that obtained using isotonic distributional regression (IDR), a recent statistical post-processing method, applied to either the ECMWF ensemble or the machine-learning models FuXi and GraphCast. Unlike IDR, cGAN generates individual ensemble-member realisations (potentially many thousands), including exceptional weather events. This ability was deemed important when assessed in an operational context by the National Meteorological and Hydrological Services of Kenya and Ethiopia. cGAN is cheap to train/run and requires no additional post-processing. It is run on laptops making it practical as a high-resolution medium-range ensemble forecast system for Meteorological Services with limited computational resources.

title: LiDAR-Constrained Multi-Temporal UAV Monitoring of Glacier Terminus Retreat and Secondary Landslide Evolution at Hailuogou Glacier, Mt. Gongga, China
abstract: Joint quantification of glacier terminus change and adjacent secondary landslide evolution can be challenging when multi-temporal UAV datasets lack a consistent absolute spatial reference, thereby limiting robust assessment of their stage-dependent covariation. This study investigated the Hailuogou glacier terminus and the Laoguanjingtai (LGJT) landslide using six UAV photogrammetric surveys acquired between 2018 and 2022 and synchronous airborne light detection and ranging (LiDAR) data from 2022. LiDAR reference constraints and elevation-residual assessment over relatively stable terrain supported multi-temporal digital elevation model (DEM) differencing. The glacier terminus area decreased from 2.63×105m2 to 1.43×105m2, representing a reduction of 45.5%. From July 2020 to August 2022, the glacier volume ablation rate reached 1.00×106m3a−1. Meanwhile, the LGJT landslide shifted from deposition-dominated adjustment from 2018 to 2019 to erosion-dominated material export after July 2020, when its erosion rate reached 3.73×105m3a−1 and its net volume change rate decreased to −3.39×105m3a−1. Annualized rates across five unequal intervals showed positive covariation between glacier ablation and landslide erosion and negative covariation with net landslide volume change. These exploratory associations, together with the spatial concentration of elevation change near the glacier–landslide margin, are consistent with a geomorphic linkage. The LiDAR-constrained UAV workflow provides a practical basis for integrated monitoring of glacier retreat and adjacent sediment redistribution.

title: Regional Snow Cover Fraction Prediction in Xinjiang Using a Terrain-Aware Graph Neural Network
abstract: Snow cover fraction (SCF) reflects the regional snow cover changes in arid mountainous areas. We developed a terrain-aware graph convolutional network–long short-term memory network (GCN-LSTM), where 9 meteorological stations in Xinjiang serve as graph nodes and 15 monthly meteorological variables as dynamic node features, while altitude, slope, and aspect define a fixed terrain information graph. The overall study period spanned March 2000–June 2022; the model uses a 12-month input window and predicts regional snow cover fraction in Xinjiang one month in advance under strict time series partitioning. On the 30-month test set (January 2020–June 2022), the model’s mean seed-level root mean square error (RMSE) was the lowest point estimate (0.0386); paired block-bootstrap intervals for ensemble-prediction differences from monthly climatology and ridge included zero. The model followed the pronounced seasonal cycle, but its five-seed ensemble had a deseasonalized anomaly R2 of −0.009, providing limited evidence of predictive skill beyond seasonality. The terrain-weighted graph had lower test RMSE than the geographic graph but similar error to the terrain-binary graph; intervals for most other graph comparisons crossed zero. Radiation accounted for 31.28% of total grouped SHAP (Shapley Additive Explanations) attribution and Lag-1 meteorological inputs for 36.24% of lag attribution. Removing the Moisture group during retrained ablation increased ensemble test RMSE by 0.0033. Different rankings indicate that attribution analysis and ablation analysis capture different aspects of model dependencies. Across seven retrospective annual outer Test folds (84 months), the ensemble did not show a stable improvement over monthly climatology (pooled RMSE 0.03896 vs.0.03763); terrain information remains a spatial prior whose broader predictive value requires further evaluation.

title: Reconciling advective upwelling with diapycnal downwelling: A transient kinematic perspective on Munk's conundrum
abstract: arXiv:2502.21006v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Bottom-intensified turbulent fluxes observed near the seafloor drive abyssal densification and diapycnal downwelling through their vertical divergence. This appears paradoxical under steady stratification because dense bottom waters continuously enter from Antarctic sources. Motivated by evolving Indo-Pacific stratification, we use idealized simulations to examine abyssal overturning under transient and steady-state conditions. Using a kinematic rather than thermodynamic water-mass-transformation approach, we diagnose advective overturning, isopycnal volume tendency, and diapycnal transport in two cooling experiments with different mixing intensities, one warming experiment, and one quasi-equilibrium experiment. Advective upwelling occurs in all four, whereas diagnosed diapycnal transport varies in direction. In Type-I cooling, the isopycnal volume tendency exceeds advective overturning in magnitude, yielding downward diapycnal transport; in Type-II cooling, advective overturning exceeds the isopycnal volume tendency, yielding upward diapycnal transport. The warming and quasi-equilibrium experiments also exhibit upward diapycnal transport. These relationships persist qualitatively in potential-temperature coordinates. Type-I cooling also spontaneously produces an observationally documented bottom-intensified buoyancy-flux profile with an e-folding scale comparable to previous estimates. Thus, cooling alone does not determine diapycnal transport direction; it depends kinematically on the relative strengths of advective overturning and isopycnal volume tendency. Within this idealized framework, the results provide a transient kinematic interpretation of the interior-downwelling conundrum: abyssal waters can rise through the basin interior while undergoing diapycnal downwelling, without requiring an upslope return pathway within the bottom boundary layer.

title: Evaluating extreme precipitation forecasts: a threshold-weighted, spatial verification approach for comparing an AI weather prediction model against a high-resolution NWP model
abstract: This study introduces a verification method that accounts for differences in grid resolution when evaluating extreme event forecasts. We apply it to an artificial intelligence-based weather prediction model and a high-resolution numerical weather prediction model. Results show that, when assessed on equivalent neighborhood scales, the high resolution numerical weather prediction model only outperforms the AI system for short lead times in predicting extreme precipitation.

title: New insights on the suitability of NetCDF/HDF5 as storage format for climate cloud repositories
abstract: Climate science is increasingly adopting cloud-based infrastructures for data access and analysis. Contrary to the widespread belief that traditional formats such as NetCDF/HDF5 are unsuitable for remote cloud access, this study demonstrates that they can perform efficiently in cloud environments. These findings challenge current assumptions and provide practical insights that could support CMIP7 data workflows while reducing the need for major changes to existing climate data infrastructures.

title: Linking the evolution of floe sizes to the sea-ice deformation  history using SAR imagery
abstract: Polar oceans are covered by many pieces of floating ice, called floes, that vary in size, shape and thickness. This study focuses on how fracturing caused by stresses from wind and ocean currents changes floe sizes. Using satellite images, we track ice motion and floe sizes, and study floe shapes and how deformation alters the distribution of floe sizes. We find that stronger deformation creates more small floes and present a formula to include this effect in sea-ice models.

title: SeidarT: an open-source full-waveform seismic and electromagnetic wave propagation modeling toolbox demonstrated in snow and ice
abstract: We developed open-source software that simulates how elastic and electromagnetic waves travel through snow and ice with the aim to advance and make accessible ice and snow imaging methods. This helps researchers test survey designs and interpret field measurements without expensive or risky expeditions. Parameters influencing the mechanics of snow and ice are easily input from JSON files, and geometries can be generated using an image editor allowing for time effective production of models.

title: Hybrid implicit–explicit XFEM simulation of injection-induced seismicity: resolving multi-scale rupture nucleation and dynamics
abstract: Injecting fluids underground for energy projects can trigger earthquakes. Predicting these events is difficult because underground pressure changes slowly, while faults can move in a fraction of a second. We developed a computer method that switches between two ways of calculating these processes. In our test, it reduced computing time by 62 % while giving similar estimates of earthquake size and total fault movement. Differences in the fastest movements show that further testing is needed.

title: Slope-Constrained Orography (SCO v1.0) for explicit discrete-slope control in terrain preprocessing: a case study with WRF-ARW (v4.6.1)
abstract: High-resolution weather models over mountains need terrain smoothing to avoid crashing, but standard methods smooth everywhere regardless of need. We developed Slope-Constrained Orography, a tool that uses one slope-angle setting to adjust only the points that are too steep. Tested over the southeastern Tibetan Plateau, stable simulations were achieved while modifying far less terrain than standard smoothing, offering a simpler approach to running weather models over steep terrain.

title: GECKO-A v1.0: exploring VOC oxidation trajectories through comparison with the master chemical mechanism
abstract: This study presents the first open-source release of a tool that automatically generates chemical mechanisms for the atmospheric oxidation of organic compounds. Simulations for five hydrocarbons, under conditions ranging from urban to remote, are compared with a benchmark mechanism. Results show that describing successive oxidation steps is key to simulating the formation of low-volatility and water-soluble species important for aerosols. A reduced mechanism reproduces most of these results.

title: Identifying Snow-Covered Areas from Unoccupied Aerial Systems (UAS) Visible Imagery and Lidar: A Comparison of Methods
abstract: Visible images from unoccupied aerial systems (UAS) can be used to map snow, especially where snow is shallow and does not last long. We tested several methods for identifying snow-covered areas using UAS images collected in southern New Hampshire, USA. We found that using the full color information gives the most reliable results. We showed how UAS surveys can be planned to create accurate snow cover maps, helping track snow in changing conditions.

title: cSINGV v1.0: development and evaluation of a 1.5 km  coupled atmosphere–ocean–wave modelling  system for the Western Maritime Continent
abstract: Weather over Southeast Asia is shaped by complex interactions between the air, ocean, and waves. We developed a high-resolution model that links these processes to better understand and predict rainfall patterns in the region. The results show that ocean–atmosphere interactions improve the representation and prediction of squall events that affect daily life in Singapore and surrounding regions. This work supports more accurate weather forecasting in the region.

title: A deep-atmosphere extension in a nonhydrostatic dynamical core: formulation and idealized tests
abstract: Many atmospheric models use shallow approximation that work well when the model top is low. As models top now reach higher layers, these approximation need to be relaxed. We develop a deep atmosphere dynamical core(GMCORE), including full deep atmosphere dynamics, and spherical geometry. The tests case with idealized baroclinic waves and tropical cyclones show that the new model reproduces known results and can alter storm trajectory, suggesting value for future high-top and tropical studies.

title: An open-source Python framework for the flexible deployment and advanced applications of the Variable Infiltration Capacity (VIC) model
abstract: Hydrological models help scientists understand water movement and predict changes in water resources. However, their increasing complexity makes them difficult to use. This study developed an open-source framework to simplify the setup and application of the Variable Infiltration Capacity model. Tests in multiple basins showed that the framework improves efficiency, provides reliable simulations, and supports wider use of hydrological models.

title: Evaluation and improvement of CAMS-derived CCN  number concentrations using in-situ measurements
abstract: Particles in the atmosphere can trigger the formation of cloud droplets, affecting cloud properties and climate. This study evaluates a new global dataset of these particles with measurements from 25 sites around the world. The variability in time and space and their conditional formation behaviour is analysed. The authors identify systematic biases and introduce a simple correction based on observations that greatly improves the dataset's accuracy.

title: PLSTM-Reg v1.0: a regional physics-encoded LSTM model for simulating reservoir operations without site-specific training
abstract: We introduce a deep learning approach that extracts shared operating patterns from diverse, data-rich reservoirs and transfers this knowledge to limited-data reservoirs, yielding skillful simulations of storage and release. Using satellite observations, the model also reconstructs historical behavior in no-data reservoirs. Together, this work provide a scalable foundation for addressing pressing data gaps in reservoir operations and better supporting large-scale and long-term water management.

title: A hybrid physics–ML framework for integrating groundwater dynamics into land surface modeling: a ParFlow-based demonstration in headwater watersheds of the Pearl River Basin, China
abstract: Groundwater strongly influences exchanges of water and energy between land and atmosphere, but detailed simulation is computationally expensive. We developed a faster approach that preserves groundwater–land surface interactions. In a representative watershed within China's Pearl River Basin, it ran 18.24 times faster while closely matching the physics-based model, offering a practical way to represent groundwater in large-scale environmental modeling.

title: Assessing cloud representation in two microphysics schemes of MPAS–Atmosphere model (version 8.2.2) over the Maritime Continent with Himawari-9 AHI observations
abstract: Rapidly evolving clouds over the tropical area, where complex terrain and tropical weather conditions interact, are difficult to predict. This study uses frequent, high-resolution Himawari-9 satellite observations to evaluate how well a weather model predicts cloud amount, cloud type, cloud height, and daily cloud changes over this region. The aim is to support future model development, improve cloud forecasts, and make better use of satellite observations in cloudy areas.

title: MSDT v1.0: an open-source multi-method snow drought toolbox
abstract: Snow droughts can threaten water supplies, ecosystems, and communities, but studies often use different methods and data, making results hard to compare. We developed an open-source Python tool that combines snow drought detection methods, data download, mapping, and standardized output in one workflow. Tests with global snow data show that the tool identifies annual, monthly, and daily events consistently. This makes snow drought studies easier to repeat, compare, and use in planning.
